title: the Vishnu Purana (selections)
tomorrow: Maitreya's first question is huge: where did the world come from?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vishnu Purana opened on Prahlada, telling his classmates the same Lord lives in each of them. Today, a step back: who's telling his story, and to whom?

Plenty of podcasts have the same bones: one voice that asks, one that knows, and the listener sitting in between. The Vishnu Purana is built that way. Nobody narrates it from above. A student named Maitreya comes to his teacher, the sage Parashara, with questions, and the whole Purana unfolds as the teacher's answers. Prahlada's story too: it's Parashara telling it to Maitreya.

The Purana opens with Maitreya bowing to Parashara and asking big things: how the world came to be, what it's made of, where it goes. Parashara says he'll tell it, and the telling becomes the book. So every story in it, Prahlada's included, is something a teacher says to a student who asked. That shape should sound familiar by now. A few days ago it was saha navavatu: teacher and student, every verb counting two, asking not to turn against each other. Here's the round of what came between. Prachodayat: the Gayatri's last word, may he stir our thoughts. Saha navavatu: a chant in the dual. Yaska's post: a load carried without knowing what it is. Dyauh shantih: peace that starts with the sky and comes to me last. Sam gacchadhvam: go together, speak together, still many voices. And Prahlada: the Lord in every being, even the rude kid in the back row. A verse, chants, a hymn and a Purana, all built around people saying something to each other.

segments.voice: On a scrap of paper, write one line from these two weeks you'd want to keep, in English or in Sanskrit. Under it, write the name of one person you'd tell it to. Then sit with the page, the line on top and the person underneath.
